 Abstract 
 Recently, self-play fine-tuning ( 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} ) has been proposed to adapt large language models to downstream applications with scarce expert-annotated data, by iteratively generating synthetic responses from the model itself. However, 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} is designed to optimize the current reward advantages of annotated responses over synthetic responses at hand, which may gradually vanish during iterations, leading to unstable optimization . Moreover, the utilization of reference policy induces a misalignment issue between the reward formulation for training and the metric for generation. To address these limitations, we propose a novel T riplet-based S elf- P lay f I ne-tu N ing ( 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} ) method that integrates two key designs. First, beyond current advantages, 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} additionally incorporates historical advantages between iteratively generated responses and proto-synthetic responses produced by the initial policy. Even if the current advantages diminish, historical advantages remain effective, stabilizing the overall optimization. Second, 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} introduces the entropy constraint into the self-play framework, which is theoretically justified to support reference-free fine-tuning, eliminating the training-generation discrepancy. Empirical results on various tasks demonstrate not only the superior performance of 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} over 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} , but also its stable evolution during iterations. Remarkably, compared to supervised fine-tuning, 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} achieves comparable or even better performance with only 25 % 25\% samples, highlighting its effectiveness when faced with scarce annotated data. 
 1 Introduction 
 Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated powerful generalization capabilities and profound impact across various fields ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Huang and Chang, 2023 ; Qin et al., 2023 ; Bai et al., 2023 ; Achiam et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2024a ; Wu et al., 2024a ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024a ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Hui et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2024a ; Jiang et al., 2024b ; Anthropic, 2024a ; Google, 2024 ; OpenAI, 2024 ; Sun et al., 2025a ; Sun et al., 2025b ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Qian et al., 2026 ) . The remarkable success of LLMs is inherently linked to the utilization of vast expert annotations. Nevertheless, considerable curation costs for high-quality data pose major obstacles to downstream-task adaptation ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Tan et al., 2024 ) . Consequently, numerous efforts have been made to handling this challenge, e.g., data augmentation ( Dai et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2024b ) and model distillation ( Gunasekar et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Xin et al., 2024 ) . 
 Recently, a promising research direction known as self-play fine-tuning has been introduced ( Chen et al., 2024b ) , and has since been applied to various LLM fields ( Yuan et al., 2024a ; Wu et al., 2024b ; Gao et al., 2024a ) . The core idea of self-play fine-tuning is to progressively refine the LLM by competing against itself. Formally, it can be framed as a two-player game between a main player and an opponent player, each of which corresponds to an instance policy of the same LLM. In this game, the main player aims to distinguish expert-annotated responses from generated ones, while the opponent player strives to produce high-quality synthetic responses that can deceive the main player. 
 Based on this framework, Chen et al. (2024b) introduce the seminal method named 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} , which is designed to optimize the relative reward advantages of annotated responses over generated ones, and employs the policy from previous iteration as a reference for reward computations. However, with the evolution of LLM, the relative advantage between two types of data gradually diminishes over time. When the relative advantage is eliminated, the optimization objective of 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} degenerates into a constant independent of the policy, allowing any policy to become an optimal solution and thus leading to unstable optimization . Moreover, the incorporation of reference policy in 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} causes a misalignment between the reward formulation used for training and the log likelihood that guides response generation. Empirical evidences in Figure  3 reveal that although annotated responses yield higher rewards than generated responses, their log likelihoods become lower than synthetic samples during iterations.
In other words, higher rewards do not necessarily lead to higher generation priority. 
 Figure 1 : Comparisons of three strategies:
(a) supervised fine-tuning requires large amounts of annotated data to train π θ \pi_{\theta} ;
(b) self-play fine-tuning operates with limited annotated data and iteratively generated samples, and employs the previous policy π θ t \pi_{\theta_{t}} as a reference for updates;
(c) triplet-based self-play fine-tuning employs triplet inputs, i.e., annotated data, synthetic samples, and proto-synthetic ones from the initial policy π θ 0 \pi_{\theta_{0}} , and updates π θ \pi_{\theta} without auxiliaries from any reference policies. 
 To address these limitations, we propose a new self-play fine-tuning method, termed T riplet-based S elf- P lay f I ne-tu N ing ( 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} ). The basic intuition is to incorporate historical advantages for stable evolution, and eliminate the reference policy for training-generation alignments. Specifically, we introduce two key modifications to the self-play framework. First, the main player is required not only to distinguish between real and synthetic data, but also discriminate proto-synthetic samples produced by the initial policy. By incorporating triplet inputs of real, synthetic and proto-synthetic samples, 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} optimizes current and historical advantages simultaneously. Even if the current advantage diminishes (i.e., synthetic samples become indistinguishable from annotated ones), the historical advantages between synthetic responses and proto-synthetic responses still exist, ensuring a stable optimization over the policy model. Second, the opponent player maximizes the confidence of synthetic responses with an entropy constraint , where the confidence measures how likely the main player believes a response comes from the annotated data. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that the incorporation of the entropy constraint removes the need for reference policy, aligning the principles of training and generation. Empirical results show that 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} consistently maintains higher log-likelihoods for annotated data compared to synthetic samples. 
 We conduct experiments on Zephyr-7B ( Tunstall et al., 2023 ) and Mistral-7B ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) , and select 50 ​ k 50k annotated samples from Ultrachat200k ( Ding et al., 2023 ) as the training set. The performance is evaluated across diverse tasks to assess multi-dimensional capabilities of LLMs, including math and logic, multi-domain knowledge, commonsense reasoning, and instruction-following. Experimental results demonstrate that 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} significantly improves performance, particularly in math and instruction-following, and achieves superior and stable performances during iterations compared to 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} . Furthermore, we also show that 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} , using only 25 % 25\% annotated samples, can achieve comparable performance (or even better on certain tasks) to supervised fine-tuning with the full training set, highlighting the effectiveness of 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} in addressing the scarcity of annotated data. 
 2 Preliminary 
 In this section, we provide a brief overview of three fine-tuning strategies (i.e., supervised fine-tuning, self-play fine-tuning, and our 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} ) for LLMs. The comparisons are also illustrated in Figure  1 . 
 2.1 Supervised fine-tuning 
 A common strategy to adapt a pretrained model to downstream tasks is fine-tuning it on high-quality annotated data. Specifically, given a prompt 𝐱 \mathbf{x} and its corresponding annotated response 𝐲 \mathbf{y} , supervised fine-tuning (SFT) aims to align the model with ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) (\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) . Formally, the goal of SFT is to learn a policy π SFT \pi_{\textrm{SFT}} by maximizing the log-likelihood of high-quality annotated data: 
 π SFT = argmax π θ 𝔼 𝐱 ∼ q ( ⋅ ) , 𝐲 ∼ π d ​ a ​ t ​ a ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) [ log π θ ( 𝐲 | 𝐱 ) ] , \pi_{\textrm{SFT}}=\argmax_{\pi_{\theta}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim q(\cdot),\mathbf{y}\sim\pi_{data}(\cdot|\mathbf{x})}\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})\right], 
 (1) 
 where q ⁡ ( ⋅ ) q(\cdot) and π d ​ a ​ t ​ a ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \pi_{data}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) denote the distributions of prompts and annotated responses, respectively. Mathematically, ( 1 ) is equivalent to the solution of minimizing the KL divergence between the target distribution π d ​ a ​ t ​ a ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \pi_{data}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) and the policy π θ ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) : 
 π SFT = argmin π θ 𝔼 𝐱 ∼ q ⁡ ( ⋅ ) [ 𝔻 KL ( π d ​ a ​ t ​ a ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) | | π θ ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) ) ] . \pi_{\textrm{SFT}}=\argmin_{\pi_{\theta}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim q(\cdot)}\left[\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{data}(\cdot|\mathbf{x})||\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}))\right]. 
 (2) 
 It can be verified that the solution ( 2 ) exactly matches the target distribution of annotated responses, i.e.,  π SFT ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) = π data ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \pi_{\textrm{SFT}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x})=\pi_{\text{data}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) . Unfortunately, achieving the optimal policy typically demands extensive high-quality samples, resulting in high costs for data curation and annotation, and thereby limiting the practical applicability of supervised fine-tuning ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Tan et al., 2024 ) . 
 2.2 Self-play fine-tuning 
 Self-play fine-tuning has emerged as a promising way to address the scarcity of expert-annotated data when adapting LLMs to downstream tasks ( Chen et al., 2024b ; Yuan et al., 2024a ) . Different from SFT that runs over a fixed annotated dataset, self-play fine-tuning employs both annotated samples and self-generated responses as inputs, with the latter continuously refined as the model evolves. 
 Specifically, at each iteration t + 1 t+1 , the model first generates a synthetic response 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} for a given prompt 𝐱 \mathbf{x} by sampling from the policy π θ t ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) . Then, the model utilizes the prompt 𝐱 \mathbf{x} and pairwise samples (i.e., the annotated response 𝐲 \mathbf{y} and the synthetic response 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} ) to obtain the policy π θ t + 1 \pi_{\theta_{t+1}} . Let the reward for a response be formulated by the log ratio of the likelihood between the current policy π θ \pi_{\theta} and the previous policy π θ t \pi_{\theta_{t}} ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) . Then, the objective of 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} ( Chen et al., 2024b ) is to maximize the gap (referred to as the relative advantage) between the reward of annotated response 𝐲 \mathbf{y} and that of synthetic response 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} : 
 π θ t + 1 = argmin π θ 𝔼 ​ [ ℓ ⁡ ( λ ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐲 | 𝐱 ) π θ t ​ ( 𝐲 | 𝐱 ) − λ ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐲 ′ | 𝐱 ) π θ t ​ ( 𝐲 ′ | 𝐱 ) ) ] , \begin{split}\pi_{\theta_{t+1}}=\argmin_{\pi_{\theta}}\mathbb{E}\left[\ell\left(\lambda\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})}{\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})}-\lambda\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}^{\prime}|\mathbf{x})}{\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\mathbf{y}^{\prime}|\mathbf{x})}\right)\right],\end{split} 
 (3) 
 where λ > 0 \lambda>0 denotes a hyper-parameter, ℓ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \ell(\cdot) is a convex and monotonically decreasing function, and the expectation operation is taken over the distributions 𝐱 ∼ q ( ⋅ ) , 𝐲 ∼ π d ​ a ​ t ​ a ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \mathbf{x}\sim q(\cdot),\mathbf{y}\sim\pi_{data}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) and 𝐲 ′ ∼ π θ t ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \mathbf{y}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) . In the following, we elaborate two major limitations of 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} : unstable optimization during iterations and misalignment between training and generation. 
 Unstable optimization. 
The instability of 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} arises from the inherent structure of the objective in ( 3 ). To be precise, we consider the case where the synthetic response 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} becomes identical to the annotated response 𝐲 \mathbf{y} (i.e., 𝐲 ′ = 𝐲 \mathbf{y}^{\prime}=\mathbf{y} ). In this case, the advantage of 𝐲 \mathbf{y} over 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} vanishes, causing the objective ( 3 ) to degenerate into a constant that is independent of the policy π θ \pi_{\theta} . As a result, any policy π θ \pi_{\theta} becomes optimal to ( 3 ), leading to unstable optimization or even performance degradation. 
 Misalignment between training and generation. 
Given the reference policy π θ t \pi_{\theta_{t}} from the iteration t t , the objective ( 3 ) is designed to optimize the reward gap between two types of responses, where the reward for a response 𝐲 ^ \hat{\mathbf{y}} is defined as r ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ^ ) = λ ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐲 ^ | 𝐱 ) − λ ​ log ⁡ π θ t ​ ( 𝐲 ^ | 𝐱 ) r(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathbf{y}})=\lambda\log\pi_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x})-\lambda\log\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x}) . However, it is important to note that the formulation of r ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ^ ) r(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathbf{y}}) differs from the principle used for generation, i.e.,  log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐲 ^ | 𝐱 ) \log\pi_{\theta}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}|\mathbf{x}) . In other words, due to the incorporation of reference policy π θ t \pi_{\theta_{t}} , a higher reward, i.e.,  r ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) > r ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐳 ) r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})>r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}) for two responses 𝐲 \mathbf{y} and 𝐳 \mathbf{z} , does not necessarily imply a higher generation probability, i.e.,  log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐲 | 𝐱 ) > log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) \log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}|\mathbf{x})>\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) may not hold. This demonstration has been empirically verified by our experiments, as illustrated in Figure  3 . 
 3 Triplet-based self-play fine-tuning 
 In this section, we introduce our triplet-based self-play fine-tuning ( 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} ), a stable and reference-free method for fine-tuning LLMs. Building upon the self-play framework, our 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} involves two players: a main player and an opponent player, both of which are different policy instances from the same LLM. For clarity, we describe the update rules for two players separately. 
 The update rule for main player. 
Recall that the goal of the main player is to distinguish among the annotated response 𝐲 \mathbf{y} , the synthetic response 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} generated from the previous policy π θ t \pi_{\theta_{t}} and the proto-synthetic response 𝐲 0 \mathbf{y}_{0} produced by the initial policy π θ 0 \pi_{\theta_{0}} . Conceptually, the triple responses are expected to satisfy the relation 𝐲 ⪰ 𝐲 ′ ⪰ 𝐲 0 \mathbf{y}\succeq\mathbf{y}^{\prime}\succeq\mathbf{y}_{0} , where the operator ⪰ \succeq indicates that the main player has greater preference for one response than in another. In other words, 𝐲 0 \mathbf{y}_{0} serves as an anchor that helps to evaluate how far the current policy π θ t \pi_{\theta_{t}} has progressed. This design is partially inspired by the schema-equilibration process in cognitive development, where knowledge builds upon and refines pre-existing cognitive anchors ( Piaget, 1952 ) . Formally, we are motivated by the integral probability metric (IPM) ( Müller, 1997 ) to establish the objective of the main player. In detail, let c ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ^ ) c(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathbf{y}}) denote the confidence with which the main player believes a response 𝐲 ^ \hat{\mathbf{y}} is sampled from the real-world data distribution π data ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \pi_{\text{data}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) . Then, the goal of main player is to find a confidence function 
 c t + 1 = argmin c ∈ 𝒞 𝔼 ​ [ ℓ ⁡ ( c ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) − c ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ′ ) ) + β ​ ℓ ​ ( c ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ′ ) − c ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 0 ) ) ] , \begin{split}c_{t+1}=\argmin_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\mathbb{E}\left[\ell\left(c(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})-c(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime})\right)+\beta\ell\left(c(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime})-c(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}_{0})\right)\right],\end{split} 
 (4) 
 where β ≥ 0 \beta\geq 0 denotes a trade-off hyper-parameter, and 𝒞 \mathcal{C} denotes a function class that will be specified later, and ℓ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \ell(\cdot) denotes a monotonically decreasing function, e.g., the logistic function ℓ ⁡ ( x ) = − log ⁡ σ ⁡ ( x ) \ell(x)=-\log\sigma(x) and the exponential function ℓ ⁡ ( x ) = exp ⁡ ( − x ) \ell(x)=\exp(-x) . The expectation operation here is taken over the distributions 𝐱 ∼ q ( ⋅ ) , 𝐲 ∼ π d ​ a ​ t ​ a ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) , 𝐲 ′ ∼ π θ t ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \mathbf{x}\sim q(\cdot),\mathbf{y}\sim\pi_{data}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{y}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) and 𝐲 0 ∼ π θ 0 ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \mathbf{y}_{0}\sim\pi_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) . Given the triple responses 𝐲 \mathbf{y} , 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} , and 𝐲 0 \mathbf{y}_{0} , the objective in ( 4 ) consists of two terms: 
 • 
 The first term ℓ ⁡ ( c ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) − c ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ′ ) ) \ell\left(c(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})-c(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime})\right) measures the gap between the real response 𝐲 ∼ π data ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \mathbf{y}\sim\pi_{\text{data}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) and the synthetic one 𝐲 ′ ∼ π θ t ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \mathbf{y}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) , reflecting the relative advantages of π data \pi_{\text{data}} over π θ t \pi_{\theta_{t}} ; 
 • 
 The second term ℓ ⁡ ( c ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ′ ) − c ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 0 ) ) \ell\left(c(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime})-c(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}_{0})\right) compares the synthetic response 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} to the proto-synthetic response 𝐲 0 ∼ π θ 0 ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \mathbf{y}_{0}\sim\pi_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) , capturing historical advantages of π θ t \pi_{\theta_{t}} over π θ 0 \pi_{\theta_{0}} during iterations. 
 During the self-play process, the opponent player evolves over time, generating synthetic responses 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} that progressively approximate the real response 𝐲 \mathbf{y} . As a result, the current advantage, i.e., the first term in ( 4 ), gradually diminishes. In contrast, since 𝐲 0 \mathbf{y}_{0} remains fixed during iterations, the historical advantage, i.e., the second term in ( 4 ), remains meaningful even when the current advantage vanishes, ensuring that ( 4 ) does not degenerate to a constant independent of π θ \pi_{\theta} . 
 The update rule for opponent player. 
In this part, we suppose that the main player has learned a confidence function c t + 1 c_{t+1} capable of effectively distinguishing between 𝐲 \mathbf{y} and 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} . Then, we proceed to elaborate on the update rule for the opponent player. Note that the goal of the opponent player is to generate a response 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} that misleads the main player to the best of its ability. Therefore, with the given confidence function c t + 1 c_{t+1} , the opponent player aims to find a policy π θ ^ \pi_{\hat{\theta}} that maximizes the expected confidence score over synthetic responses 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} generated from itself: 
 π θ ^ = argmax π θ 𝔼 𝐱 ∼ q ( ⋅ ) , 𝐲 ′ ∼ π θ ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) [ c t + 1 ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ′ ) ] + α 𝔼 𝐱 ∼ q ⁡ ( ⋅ ) [ ℋ ( π θ ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) ) ] , \begin{split}\pi_{\hat{\theta}}=&\argmax_{\pi_{\theta}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim q(\cdot),\mathbf{y}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|\mathbf{x})}\left[c_{t+1}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime})\right]+\alpha\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim q(\cdot)}\left[\mathcal{H}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}))\right],\end{split} 
 (5) 
 where α > 0 \alpha>0 denotes the regularization parameter, and ℋ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{H}(\cdot) denotes the entropy constraint. In ( 5 ), the first part reflects the confidence that how the main player believes that 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} is sampled from the real-world distribution π d ​ a ​ t ​ a \pi_{data} , and the second part serves to stabilize the optimization. It is worth noting that ( 5 ) has a closed-form solution, as stated below. 
 Proposition 1 . 
 Given a general confidence function c t + 1 c_{t+1} , the optimal policy of the opponent player in ( 5 ) takes the form of 
 π ∗ ​ ( 𝐲 ′ | 𝐱 ) = exp ⁡ ( c t + 1 ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ′ ) / α ) ∑ 𝐳 ∈ 𝒴 exp ⁡ ( c t + 1 ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐳 ) / α ) \pi^{*}(\mathbf{y}^{\prime}|\mathbf{x})=\frac{\exp(c_{t+1}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{\prime})/\alpha)}{\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{Y}}\exp(c_{t+1}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})/\alpha)} 
 where 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} denotes the set that contains all possible responses for the prompt 𝐱 \mathbf{x} . 
 Note that due to the generality of c t + 1 c_{t+1} , the closed-form solution π ∗ ​ ( 𝐲 ′ | 𝐱 ) \pi^{*}(\mathbf{y}^{\prime}|\mathbf{x}) may not be attainable in the policy space of LLM. To resolve this issue, we need to choose a specific form of the function class 𝒞 \mathcal{C} such that the closed-form solution becomes tractable . Specifically, we hope to find a policy π θ \pi_{\theta} that satisfies π θ ​ ( 𝐲 ′ | 𝐱 ) = π ∗ ​ ( 𝐲 ′ | 𝐱 ) \pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}^{\prime}|\mathbf{x})=\pi^{*}(\mathbf{y}^{\prime}|\mathbf{x}) with the confidence c t + 1 c_{t+1} learned from a certain class 𝒞 \mathcal{C} .  Comparisons between 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} and 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} . 
Both methods are designed to handle the limited available data when adapting LLMs to downstream tasks, but they fundamentally differ in (i) optimization principles, (ii) implicit reward formulation, and (iii) computational overhead, as detailed below: 
 • 
 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} only optimizes the current advantage between the annotated response 𝐲 ∼ π d ​ a ​ t ​ a ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \mathbf{y}\sim\pi_{data}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) and the synthetic response 𝐲 ′ ∼ π θ t ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \mathbf{y}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) in ( 3 ), which may result in the instability issue during iterations.
In contrast, 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} optimizes not only the current advantage of 𝐲 \mathbf{y} over 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} , but also the historical advantage of 𝐲 ′ \mathbf{y}^{\prime} over the proto-synthetic response 𝐲 0 ∼ π θ 0 ( ⋅ | 𝐱 ) \mathbf{y}_{0}\sim\pi_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}) , ensuring a stable evolution and thereby mitigating the unstable optimization; 
 • 
 In 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} , the reward function for a response 𝐳 \mathbf{z} is formulated as r θ ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) = λ ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) − λ ​ log ⁡ π θ t ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) r_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})=\lambda\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})-\lambda\log\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) . This formulation misaligns with the generation metric (i.e., the log-likelihood), resulting in potential suboptimal performance. By contrast, the reward function in 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} (also referred to as the confidence function under the self-play framework) is defined as r θ ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) = α ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) r_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})=\alpha\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) , which matches the generation metric and thus resolves the misalignment issue; 
 • 
 Compared to 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} , 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} incurs only a marginal increase in computational and memory costs. Specifically, 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} performs a one-time generation of 𝐲 0 \mathbf{y}_{0} at the beginning, which is not repeated in subsequent iterations. In practice, the costs of this generation is negligible compared to the iterative training process. Moreover, while 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} expands each training instance from a pair of ( 𝐲 , 𝐲 ′ ) (\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}^{\prime}) to a triplet of ( 𝐲 , 𝐲 ′ , 𝐲 0 ) (\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}^{\prime},\mathbf{y}_{0}) , the overall memory costs remains nearly unchanged, as it eliminates the need for a reference model, which is necessary in 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} . Consequently, the additional overhead of 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} is minimal compared to 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} .
